title: The monastery day
hook: bells, psalms, work, bread and books, all day, every day

segments.voice: Yesterday, the synod: the Church gathering to listen before it decides. Your line was walking together. Now we step back into the middle ages.

A bell rings in the dark. Nobody in the house owns an alarm clock; the bell is the clock. The monks get up, walk a covered passage around a square garden, and go into church to sing psalms. Later the same bell sends them to the fields, the kitchen, the copying desk, the table for bread, and finally to bed. The next day it starts again. Houses like this stood in valleys and on hilltops, and that covered walk they crossed again and again has a name: the cloister.
screen: `A BELL RINGS IN THE DARK.` → `PSALMS, FIELDS, BREAD, BED.` → `THE COVERED WALK.`

segments.voice: A cloister is the enclosed walk at the heart of a monastery, covered sides around an open garden, joining the church, the dining hall, the workrooms and the dormitory. The word also names the whole enclosed life: when Catholics say a nun is cloistered, they mean she lives inside that enclosure. The houses that kept the Rule of Saint Benedict had a plan behind those walls. The Rule asks that a monastery, if it can, hold everything it needs inside, water, a mill, a garden, workshops, so the monks need not wander outside, which it says does their souls no good. It calls the monastery a school for the Lord's service. Then the bell. The Rule builds the day around prayer in common, which it calls the work of God, and says nothing is to be put before it. For the hours of prayer, Benedict leans on a psalm, in the Douay-Rheims: "Seven times a day I have given praise to thee." When the signal sounds, the monk sets down whatever is in his hands and goes. And the bread. Work isn't the opposite of prayer here. Idleness, the Rule says, is the enemy of the soul, so the brothers work with their hands and read at set times. Even the kitchen is shared: the brothers serve one another by turns, and no one is excused except for sickness or more pressing work. So a cloister was never only about walls. It was a shape for a day, psalms and books, bells and bread, hardly changing from one Monday to the next. Monasteries keep that shape still. Visit one at dusk, and the bell may well be ringing.
screen: `THE WALK AT THE MONASTERY'S HEART.` · `EVERYTHING WITHIN THE WALLS.` · `NOTHING BEFORE THE WORK OF GOD.` · `IDLENESS IS THE ENEMY OF THE SOUL.` · then, large: `BELLS AND BREAD.`

segments.voice: Imagine a bell has just sounded, and let your hands go still, as if you were setting down a pen in the middle of a word. Breathe. If you pray, borrow the psalm's line, seven times a day I have given praise to thee; if you don't, just notice that you stopped.
Cloister. The covered walk at a monastery's heart, and the enclosed life around it, where bells and bread set the shape of the day. Today's word.
Your line: bells and bread. Prayer and work, held in one ordered day. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholic monks and nuns who follow the Rule of Saint Benedict pray the Liturgy of the Hours together at set times through the day, with work, reading and shared meals in between; visitors are often welcome at the sung hours.
